questions.q: In a real SOC, what form does Post-Incident Activity's "lessons learned" step actually take?
options: A scheduled meeting with a defined attendee list and agenda, held soon after the incident closes
An optional comment left on the closed incident ticket, with no set attendees
An annual review covering the entire year's incidents at once
A step that only happens if the incident made the news
questions.explain: The lessons learned review is a real, scheduled meeting — not an informal note or a once-a-year formality.

questions.q: Why does NIST recommend holding the lessons learned meeting within days of an incident's resolution rather than weeks later?
options: The timeline, decisions made, and friction points are still fresh and accurately remembered
Company policy requires all meetings to happen within 24 hours of any event
Waiting longer is against the law in most jurisdictions
There is no real reason — the timing doesn't matter
questions.explain: Wait too long and details blur — nobody remembers exactly why a step was slow or what a tool was missing.

questions.q: What are the three core questions a lessons learned meeting asks about the response?
options: What worked, what didn't, and what should change
Who is to blame, how much it cost, and when it will happen again
What tools were used, who approved them, and what they cost
Was the incident reported on time, and to whom
questions.explain: Those three questions, asked about every phase of the response, are the real agenda of the meeting.

questions.q: Who should be in the room for a lessons learned meeting, according to this lesson?
options: Everyone who touched the incident — analysts, engineers who executed containment, the affected system owner, and often management
Only the single analyst who first triaged the alert
Only senior management, with no analysts present
Only external vendors, since internal staff can't be objective
questions.explain: A useful review pulls in everyone involved, including whoever can actually approve the fixes it produces.

questions.q: In the business email compromise example, what specific "what didn't work" finding came out of the meeting?
options: The team lost over an hour confirming MFA status because no one on the call had direct access to check it
The SIEM failed to generate any alert at all
The attacker was never identified
The VP's account was never actually compromised
questions.explain: That delay, captured because the meeting happened, became a concrete action item: giving the on-call analyst direct MFA-status access.
